dietEvidence.body: The deep rostral beak and leaf-shaped teeth indicate herbivory. The jaw apparatus is consistent with cropping vegetation, but no gut contents are known; the plants eaten and the feeding mechanics remain inferences.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: A small early ceratopsian with a parrot-like beak and a relatively large head. Some specimens preserve a tail fringe and integument.
summary: A small early ceratopsian with a parrot-like beak and a relatively large head. Some specimens preserve a tail fringe and integument.

discovery.body: Named by Osborn, 1923. The record is known from Yixian and Jehol groups. Hundreds of skeletons, including juveniles and soft-tissue impressions.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: Hundreds of skeletons, including juveniles and soft-tissue impressions.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Yixian and Jehol groups records the species in the Early Cretaceous. The numeric range used here is ≈126–101 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The skull is deep and short, with a strong rostral beak. The tail bears a dorsal row of bristle-like appendages in bundles; the rest of the body is covered in scales. The bristles are preserved as carbonaceous impressions and are not true feathers.

anatomy.title: Body plan
anatomy.body: The species is reconstructed as facultatively bipedal. The posture is inferred from limb proportions and comparison with other ceratopsians, not observed.

behaviour.body: The tail bristles are direct evidence of integument, but their function is unresolved. Mayr et al. (2016) found them in bundles of three to six and noted that they covered only part of the tail, which argues against a simple insulation function; display is a hypothesis. No nesting or social evidence is asserted.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from hundreds of skeletons, including juveniles and soft-tissue impressions. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: The growth series and tail bristles are directly studied, but the bristles' function is not established. Erickson & Tumanova (2000) reconstructed an S-shaped growth curve from long-bone histology; Mayr et al. (2016) found bundles of bristles with a pulp cavity and considered them probably homologous with filamentous structures in other dinosaurs, while noting that a follicle has not been demonstrated. Body colour and social behaviour are not established here.
